params.require: N % D != 0 and 5 * abs(2 * (N % D) - D) >= D
params.why: the final rounding to 2 decimal places must really change the value, and the value must not lie close to the halfway point between two cents

stem: Given $i=\frac{r}{600}$ ; $r={=rtxt}$ ; $n={=n}$ ; $P={=P}$ . Calculate $i$ correct to ${=dp}$ decimal places. Then use this rounded value of $i$ to calculate $A$ in $A=P(1+i)^{n}$ , correct to $2$ decimal places.
solution: Round $i$ to ${=dp}$ decimal places. The digits up to decimal place ${=dp}$ are kept and the next digit is ${=d}$ . A digit of $5$ or more rounds the last kept digit up by $1$ ; a smaller digit leaves it as it is. So $i\approx{=ir}$ .
Use the rounded value of $i$ in the formula, without rounding again until the end: $\begin{aligned}A&=P(1+i)^{n}\\&={=P}\left(1+{=ir}\right)^{{=n}}\\&\approx{=Aapprox}\end{aligned}$
For comparison, working with the unrounded value of $i$ all the way through gives $A\approx{=Xs}$ , so rounding $i$ early changed the answer by ${=ds}$ .
notes: Standard step up from the basic family: round a value in the middle of the working, then USE the rounded value in a further calculation (the book's ex1-2-4a followed by ex1-2-4b, merged into one question so that the single answer A depends on the rounding of i). Same formulae as the book (i = r/600, A = P(1+i)^n) and the same two roundings; n is kept to 2, 3 or 4 (the book's 96 is not hand- or mental-checkable) and r runs over one-decimal values 3.1 to 14.9 leaving out the multiples of 0.3 and the whole numbers, so i = r/600 is a non-terminating decimal that is never exactly a rounding tie (the '...' in step 1 is always true, and the displayed value is i TRUNCATED to 5 decimal places, never rounded). i is rounded to 2 or 3 decimal places, stated in the stem. Everything is computed in exact integer arithmetic: k is the rounded i in units of 10^-dp, N/D is A in whole cents before the final rounding. The require keeps A away from the halfway point between two cents by at least 0.1 of a cent and ensures the last rounding really changes the value. Step 5 repeats the book's own lesson (ex1-2-4c: rounding i early changes the answer) with the figure computed exactly from the unrounded i = r/600; it is not asked for in the stem, so it cannot affect the answer. The stem tells the student to use the rounded value of i; this is the only reading under which the answer is a single number. Checked offline with Decimal arithmetic for 20 000 draws: the answer, the 4-decimal intermediate value, the unrounded comparison value and the difference all agree; the difference is never 0.
